title: A Cognitive Process Theory of Writing (Spanish translation: La teoria de la redaccion como proceso cognitivo, in Textos en contexto 1, Lectura y Vida)
claim: Composing is a goal-directed thinking process, guided by the writer's own growing hierarchical network of goals: writers set high-level goals and supporting sub-goals, and sometimes change or regenerate the high-level goals based on what they learn while writing. The authors PREDICT (not demonstrate) that the amount and quality of middle-range goals, which sit between intention and prose, will be a key difference between good and poor writers. Many goals are well-learned and stored in memory (e.g. 'interest the reader', 'start with the introduction', genre goals) rather than generated for the piece. The writer's goals/plan, topic knowledge and the text so far compete for control: e.g. a vivid opening sentence can demand a cause next, violating a planned three-point paragraph; such collaboration often ends in revising earlier goals. Original: College Composition and Communication 32(4):365-387, 1981.

title: Cognitive Operations in Constructing Main Points in Written Composition (Journal of Memory and Language 27, 261-278)
authors: Carl Bereiter, P. J. Burtis, Marlene Scardamalia
claim: In knowledge-telling, coherence and organization come as a by-product of procedures that generate content, not from problem solving aimed at them; a level-1 main point is typically a by-product of retrieving content cued by the assignment and genre. Knowledge-transforming subordinates content generation to two problem spaces: a content space (belief, logical consistency) and a rhetorical space (goals of the composition). Goals in one space translate into problems in the other: a rhetorical goal (strengthen an argument) becomes a content problem (find an example), which can revise the belief and then the original rhetorical goal. Building a main point in this model means deliberately pursuing it as a goal. In experiment 2, younger students' choices and justifications suggested they had not intended to produce a main point.

title: Minto Pyramid Principle: Concept
claim: The concept page says people work out their thinking by building pyramids of ideas. They group similar low-level facts, draw an insight from each group, and group related insights again until the thinking ends as a single pyramid that obeys logical rules and is held together by one thought. Communicating it means guiding the reader down the pyramid from the top. The course page (barbaraminto.com/course) says the method starts by identifying the reader's question, including in complex cases. 'SCQ Framework' appears only as a site header and tagline and is not defined on either page.

title: The Craft of Research, Fifth Edition (publisher page and table of contents)
authors: Wayne C. Booth, Gregory G. Colomb, Joseph M. Williams, Joseph Bizup, William T. FitzGerald
claim: Per the publisher's table of contents (5th ed., 2024; Booth, Colomb, Williams, Bizup, FitzGerald): Part III 'Making Your Argument' has chapters on an argument overview (5), claims (6), reasons and evidence (7), warrants (8), and acknowledgments and responses (9). Section 5.5 is 'Planning Your Research Argument' and chapter 10 'Planning and Drafting' has 'Planning Your Paper' before 'Turning Your Plan into a Draft'. Chapter 11 'Revising and Organizing' has sections on revising the frame (11.2), the argument (11.3) and the organization (11.4), and on checking paragraphs (11.5).

title: The Science of Scientific Writing (American Scientist 78(6):550-558), reproduced on Tom Verhoeff's site
authors: George D. Gopen, Judith A. Swan
claim: Readers expect fixed places for information. The topic position (sentence start) should hold old information that links backward. The stress position (sentence end) holds the new material meant for emphasis. A unit of discourse is anything with a beginning and an end (clause, sentence, section, article). Each unit, whatever its size, is expected to serve one function and make one point. Placing information where readers expect it gives the writer far greater, but never complete, control over interpretation. The structure of the prose becomes the structure of the scientific argument.

title: Revising for Style: Cohesion and Coherence (Duke Writing Studio handout; recommends Williams, Style: The Basics of Clarity and Grace)
authors: Duke Thompson Writing Program / Writing Studio, drawing on Joseph M. Williams
claim: Duke Writing Studio handout 'Revising for Style: Cohesion and Coherence' (Feb 2023). Cohesion is sentence-by-sentence flow: the topic position (start) holds old, familiar information and the stress position (end) holds new information. Coherence is overall unity, covering both sentence topics and each paragraph's main point. The example passage is called cohesive (each sentence connects, old first, new last) but not coherent: each sentence's topic differs from the one before, so the paragraph lacks focus. The handout lists Williams's 'Style: The Basics of Clarity and Grace' under 'Books on Style'.

title: Extraction and Evaluation of Formulaic Expressions Used in Scholarly Papers (section on Swales's moves)
authors: Kenichi Iwatsuki, Florian Boudin, Akiko Aizawa
claim: Iwatsuki, Boudin and Aizawa (arXiv 2020) say Swales (1981) first introduced the move: a rhetorical unit that conveys a communicative function in scholarly papers. Moves follow an order set by the research community, their transitions are fixed to some extent, and each move has finer-grained steps. His later work (1981, 1990, 2004) focused on introductions; Cotos et al. and Maswana et al. (2015) extended move analysis to every section. The units that carry a function are flexible: several sentences can carry one function, and so can a clause. Earlier NLP work treated a sentence as the unit of function, and this paper adopts the same assumption.

title: Evaluating Arguments Based on Toulmin's Scheme (Argumentation 19:347-371)
authors: Bart Verheij (on Stephen Toulmin, The Uses of Argument, 1958)
claim: Toulmin's layout extends the premises-conclusion model with warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal. The Data are facts that support the Claim. The Warrant is an inference license by which the Data support the Claim. Backing supports the Warrant. A Rebuttal gives conditions of exception, and the Qualifier expresses the degree of certainty. Verheij says Toulmin discussed only the structure of arguments, not their evaluation. He adds evaluation by dialectical interpretation: a statement can be justified, defeated (contra-justified), or neither.

title: An Introduction to Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST website)
authors: William C. Mann, Maite Taboada (on Mann & Thompson 1988)
claim: RST explains coherence as every part of a text having an evident role, with no parts missing. Spans are related, virtually always adjacent ones, most often as nucleus and satellite, and an analysis's combinations of spans and relations cover the entire text. Each relation is defined by constraints on the nucleus, the satellite and their combination, plus an effect the author intends in the reader, which is never empty. So every observed relation ascribes an intention to the author, and an analysis that gives every span a role ascribes a reason for every element. Nothing in RST forces a role for every element, but carefully written texts virtually always get one. A text may have more than one valid analysis.

title: The Rhetorical Situation (Philosophy & Rhetoric 1:1-14; 1992 reprint)
claim: Rhetorical discourse is called into existence by a situation and is rhetorical insofar as it works as a fitting response to it. The situation controls the response the way a question controls its answer. There are three parts: an exigence (an imperfection marked by urgency that discourse can modify), an audience (people able to be influenced and to act as mediators of change), and constraints (beliefs, attitudes, documents, facts, traditions, interests, motives; the rhetor adds personal character, logical proofs and style). In any rhetorical situation at least one controlling exigence acts as the organizing principle: it specifies the audience to be addressed and the change to be made.

title: Comprehension and the Given-New Contract (in Freedle, ed., Discourse Production and Comprehension, Ablex)
authors: Herbert H. Clark, Susan E. Haviland
claim: Under the given-new contract the speaker conveys what the listener already knows as given and what the listener does not yet know as new. The heart of the contract is the maxim of antecedence: the listener should have exactly one direct antecedent for any given information, and it should be the intended one. The listener's three steps are: separate given from new, search memory for a direct antecedent, then attach the new information to it. When no direct antecedent exists, the listener bridges by inference, adds a new node, or restructures given and new. Restructuring is for unintended or covert violations. A deliberate violation, such as 'The old woman died' opening a story, signals that the listener should assume the referent exists, which is often used as a literary device.

title: Attention, Intentions, and the Structure of Discourse (Computational Linguistics 12(3):175-204)
authors: Barbara J. Grosz, Candace L. Sidner
claim: Discourse structure has three separate but related parts: linguistic structure (the segments of utterances), intentional structure (a structure of purposes) and attentional state (the focus of attention). Each segment has a discourse segment purpose (DSP) that specifies how the segment contributes to the overall discourse purpose (DP). Two structural relations hold between purposes: dominance (DSP1 contributes to DSP2, so DSP2 dominates DSP1, which builds a hierarchy) and satisfaction-precedence (DSP1 must be satisfied before DSP2). There are infinitely many possible intentions but only a small number of structural relations between them.

title: Revision Strategies of Student Writers and Experienced Adult Writers (College Composition and Communication 31(4):378-388)
claim: Sommers coded revisions by four operations (deletion, substitution, addition, reordering) and four levels (word, phrase, sentence, theme). Students mostly made lexical changes (a 'thesaurus philosophy'), and they lacked strategies for handling the whole essay, reordering lines of reasoning, or questioning purpose and readers. Experienced writers described their main revision goal as finding the form or shape of their argument. They treated revision as part of discovering meaning, driven by recognizing and resolving dissonance between intention and execution. The parts-whole relationship destroys the linear model of writing.

title: Reverse Outlining (Howe Writing Center handout)
claim: After drafting, the writer copies the thesis, the first and last sentence of each body paragraph, and the key concluding sentence into a blank document, which gives a skeletal version of the paper. Guiding questions ask whether the thesis matches the conclusion, whether body sentences support the thesis, and whether paragraphs connect or are disconnected. If they do not match, the writer ties the arguments back to the thesis or alters the thesis to fit them. A worked example labels each paragraph 'Paragraph says' (content) and 'Paragraph does' (function, e.g. Introduction and Thesis, Example/evidence). Its revision notes flag an undeveloped planned point and an unexplained link to the main idea.

title: Letter to A. S. Lazarev (Gruzinsky), 1 November 1889 (Polnoe sobranie sochinenii i pisem, Letters vol. 3, Nauka 1976, pp. 273-275)
claim: In his letter to A. S. Lazarev (Gruzinsky) of 1 November 1889 (PSSP, Letters vol. 3, Nauka 1976, pp. 273-275, letter 707), Chekhov says Dasha's monologue, which promises the audience a lot, would fit only if it were tied to the play's content or effects. Dasha is only a walk-on, so it is better that she stay silent altogether. You cannot put a loaded rifle on stage if nobody means to fire it. 'Нельзя обещать.' Editorial note 7 gives Gurlyand's 1904 recollection of the oral version: a pistol hung on the wall in act one must fire in the last act, otherwise do not hang it.

title: The Art of Dramatic Writing, ch. I 'Premise' (Simon and Schuster; Digital Library of India scan on archive.org)
claim: Every play needs a single premise made of character, conflict and conclusion. It gives the main character their traits, and the play grows from it like a plant from a seed. A play with more than one premise is confused. You can add a subpremise that enlarges the original. If you change your premise, you must go back to the beginning and rewrite the synopsis in its terms.

title: How to Write a Novel Using the Snowflake Method
claim: Ten steps grow outward from a one-sentence summary. Steps 1-8 produce design documents: a one-paragraph summary, one-page character summaries, one-page and four-page synopses, character synopses, full character charts, and a scene spreadsheet with one line per scene (POV and description columns). Step 9, narrative scene descriptions, is optional and the author no longer does it. Step 10 is the first draft. He says it is always okay to go back and revise earlier stages, and expects to revise steps 1-6 as the characters become real. About midway through the first draft he stops to fix the broken parts of the design documents.

title: How to Give Maris Hives, Alphabetized
claim: The Frasier bible was scrupulously maintained to record everything established about the characters and their history, such as Frasier's mother's name, Niles' favorite professor, Martin's favorite bar, and a list of Maris's food allergies that was perhaps fifty items long. Writers used it to keep the show consistent. Shows often rely on writers' assistants or script coordinators to be 'walking bibles'.

title: Chicago Manual of Style Online: Style Sheets (help page)
claim: Users can build their own style sheets for a project. Each has a title and an optional 'Applies To' field, such as an author or project title. A sheet can hold text copied from the Manual, live links to specific Manual paragraphs, and the user's own notes.

title: Professional Editorial Standards 2024, Part D Copy Editing (with Part B Structural Editing)
claim: Under D2 Consistency, standard D2.1 says to develop a style sheet, or follow one that is provided, to track, identify and consistently apply editorial style (abbreviations, numbers, spelling variety). D2.3 says to resolve variations in terminology, logic and mechanics. In the structural editing part, B1.1 says to reorganize material for a coherent structure and sequence and a logical progression of ideas, shaped for audience, medium and purpose. B2.1 says to determine which content is suitable and optimal for the audience, medium and purpose.

title: Editorial Services Definitions
claim: Developmental editors deal with content, organization and genre, and may deliver a revision ('editorial' or 'edit') letter that outlines the big-picture issues and offers suggestions for how to address them. Line editors work at the sentence or paragraph level. Copyediting includes preparing the style sheets that guide consistency and accuracy across the manuscript.

title: Message architecture (entry in The Language of Content Strategy, XML Press)
claim: Bloomstein defines a message architecture as a hierarchy of communication goals that reflect a shared vocabulary. Her example for a financial institution has a top-level attribute 'Respected' with sub-attributes such as 'Relevant' and 'Trusted'. It is a strategic foundation and yardstick for measuring content, used to plan creation, assign responsibilities, establish guidelines, assess quality and audit for redundancy.

title: Create a Content Compass (excerpt from The Content Strategy Toolkit)
claim: The core strategy statement answers what content to produce, procure, curate and share; whom it is for; why those audiences need it; and what business outcomes it supports. You then use it to make content decisions. A messaging framework (first impression, value statement, proof points) says what audiences should know and believe, and each piece of content is checked against it. Content that does not fit doesn't belong or needs to be revised.

title: TBX Elements Reference (TermBase eXchange, ISO 30042)
claim: A TBX termbase entry nests by concept (conceptEntry), then language (langSec, with required xml:lang), then term (termSec). Auxiliary information (descrip, note, admin, ref, xref, transacGrp) can attach at the concept, language or term level. A transacGrp holds one transac, whose required type attribute names a data category, followed by optional date, note, ref, transacNote and xref.

title: XLIFF Version 2.1, OASIS Standard: note element and comment annotation
claim: <notes> can appear on a file, group or unit. Each <note> has optional id, appliesTo (source or target), category (free text) and priority (integer 1-10, default 1, where 1 is the highest and can be read as an alert). A comment annotation either holds its text in a value attribute or, when value is absent, must use ref to point to a note within the same enclosing unit. The glossary module element is allowed only inside a unit.

title: What Kinds of Writing Have a Future? (SIGDOC Lifetime Achievement Award speech)
claim: Horn cut textbooks into single sentences and asked what function each performed. That gave him about 40 categories, which reliably sort about 80 percent of a subject's sentences. He grouped them into information blocks under four principles: chunking (one kind of functional meaning per chunk), relevancy (one main point by purpose or function), labeling (a label on every chunk) and consistency (the same principles for all blocks in the document). A topic-by-block-type matrix exposes gaps in knowledge.

title: Diátaxis: How to use Diátaxis (workflow) and The compass
claim: Do not create empty structures for tutorials, how-to guides, reference and explanation, and avoid top-down planning. Choose any piece (even a sentence), assess which user need it serves and how well, decide one next improvement, do it and publish or commit it, then repeat. Good structure develops from within. The compass page says its two questions (action or cognition, acquisition or application) can be applied to a whole document or at the level of sentences and words.

title: Google developer documentation style guide: About this guide (and word list)
claim: Precedence runs from project-specific style (exceptions and product-specific terms), to the Google guide, to third-party references: Merriam-Webster for spelling, Chicago Manual of Style 17th ed. for nontechnical style, and the Microsoft Writing Style Guide for technical style. Depart from the guide when that improves your content, but be consistent throughout the document. Word list entries give a directive and often alternatives, some with Recommended/Not recommended examples, and most sampled entries state no reason.

title: Design Rationale Systems: Understanding the Issues
claim: Lee (IEEE Expert, May/June 1997) splits rationale into three layers: a decision layer with five sublayers (issue, argument, alternative, evaluation, criteria; with criteria constructs the system can update evaluations when the relevant criteria change), a design artifact layer, and a design intent layer (goals, intents, requirements; criteria can be derived from goals, so when goals change the system can update or flag criteria as outdated). He lists four ways to produce rationale, ordered by system participation: reconstruction, record-and-replay, methodological byproduct, and apprentice (the system asks the designer to justify actions that differ from its expectations). Under reconstruction he cites Conklin and Burgess Yakemovic's gIBIS use at NCR, where reconstruction found design omissions that would have cost three to six times more than capturing and reconstructing the rationale. Separately, he argues a cost-effective system becomes more problematic when the cost bearer is not the beneficiary, citing Grudin that many groupware systems fail from this mismatch.

title: Hypermedia Support for Argumentation-Based Rationale: 15 Years on from gIBIS and QOC (KMI-05-18; chapter in Rationale Management in Software Engineering, 2006)
authors: Simon Buckingham Shum, Albert Selvin, Maarten Sierhuis, Jeffrey Conklin, Charles Haley, Bashar Nuseibeh
claim: The creators of gIBIS and QOC say the 'intrusive' nature of argument notations was an obstacle to adoption, and that activity declined after the first DR book in 1996 as the difficulty of embedding argumentation-based rationale in work practice sank in. They call the capture problem the central difficulty and, citing Grudin, say no designer will enter rationale only for an unknown future reader, so there must be immediate value ('value now, value later'). Compendium answers with real-time mapping by a facilitator (Dialogue Mapping), issue templates and tags. Its maps are views onto a relational database; a node can appear in multiple views, and corrections to a node update in every context where it appears.

title: Analysing the Usability of a Design Rationale Notation (KMi tech report KMI-95-13)
claim: Two empirical studies of designers using the QOC notation frame the problem as reducing design rationale's representational overheads. The second study finds an argumentation model built on laying out discrete, competing Options inappropriate when designers work in a depth-first, evolutionary mode, developing a single, complex Option.

title: Design Space Analysis (EuroPARC / Naver Labs Europe project history page for QOC, MacLean, Young, Bellotti, Moran 1991)
authors: Allan MacLean, Victoria Bellotti et al. (Rank Xerox EuroPARC)
claim: Design Space Analysis uses QOC to map the design space around an artifact: Questions highlight key issues, Options answer them, and Criteria argue for or against options through positive (solid) or negative (dotted) links, so others can understand why the resulting design is the way it is. The page says understanding what the rationale is for and who will use it is critical to justify the effort committed.

title: Documenting Architecture Decisions
claim: Nygard (15 Nov 2011) proposes short, sequentially numbered records (title, context, decision, status, consequences) kept in the project repository under doc/arch/adr-NNN.md. A reversed decision is kept and marked superseded, with a reference to its replacement. He argues large documents are never kept up to date and nobody reads them, while small, modular documents have at least a chance of being updated.

title: MADR: Markdown Architectural Decision Records (template v4)
claim: The MADR template has Context and Problem Statement, optional Decision Drivers, Considered Options, Decision Outcome, optional Consequences, optional Confirmation (how compliance can be confirmed, e.g. a design/code review or a test with a library such as ArchUnit), optional Pros and Cons of the Options, and More Information. Optional front matter covers status, date, decision-makers, consulted and informed. Files go in docs/decisions/NNNN-title-with-dashes.md with sequential numbers.

title: Literate Programming (The Computer Journal 27(2))
claim: In WEB, one source feeds WEAVE (documentation) and TANGLE (program), so the two are consistent. WEB programs are broken into small serially numbered sections, each with optional commentary then optional code. System-dependent changes go in a separate change file of 'replace x1..xm by y1..yn' edits; an error is given if the replaced lines do not match exactly, and WEAVE can optionally print only the sections actually affected by the change file.

title: An Analysis of the Requirements Traceability Problem
claim: Based on empirical studies with over 100 practitioners, most problems attributed to poor requirements traceability come from inadequate pre-requirements-specification traceability (where a requirement came from and how it evolved). Provider problems include an imbalance between the work involved and benefits gained, and structured traces provide no guarantee they are up to date. The most useful pre-RS information was the requirement's ultimate source and the people involved in its inclusion and refinement, which implies both eager generation (during production) and lazy generation on need by those originally responsible.

title: Link validity (IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management / DOORS Next 7.2 docs)
claim: In IBM Engineering Lifecycle Management 7.2 (DOORS Next, Engineering Test Management), link validity says whether a link's meaning is satisfied by the content of its two artifacts: statuses are Suspect, Valid, Invalid, plus Unknown when validity cannot be read; a link with no validity statement is implicitly suspect. Changing an artifact creates a new version and links to it become suspect; since 7.0.3 only attributes marked Affects Link Validity count. Team members set Valid or Invalid and can add comments on why. A status set in one configuration is refreshed in other configurations containing the same two artifacts with the same content and link type.

title: Event-Based Traceability for Managing Evolutionary Change (IEEE TSE 29(9))
authors: Jane Cleland-Huang, Carl K. Chang, Mark Christensen
claim: Per the abstract, traceability infrastructure tends to erode over a system's lifetime as time-pressured practitioners fail to consistently maintain links and update impacted artifacts after each change, even with automated support. The paper proposes event-notification traceability: artifacts are no longer tightly coupled but linked through an event service, so change is handled more efficiently and artifacts and links are kept in a restorable state.

title: A Large-Scale Empirical Study on Code-Comment Inconsistencies (ICPC 2019)
authors: Fengcai Wen, Csaba Nagy, Gabriele Bavota, Michele Lanza
claim: Per the abstract, the authors mined about 1.3 billion AST-level changes from the complete histories of 1,500 systems and manually analyzed 500 commits to build a taxonomy of code-comment inconsistencies fixed by developers. Results show which code change types trigger comment updates, where inconsistencies are likely to be introduced, and what kinds developers fix.

title: /* iComment: Bugs or Bad Comments? */ (SOSP 2007)
authors: Lin Tan, Ding Yuan, Gopal Krishna, Yuanyuan Zhou
claim: iComment extracts implicit program rules from natural-language comments and uses them to detect comment-code inconsistencies. On Linux, Mozilla, Wine and Apache it found 60 inconsistencies: 33 new bugs and 27 bad comments.

title: What Makes a Good Commit Message? (ICSE 2022)
authors: Yingchen Tian, Yuxia Zhang, Klaas-Jan Stol, Lin Jiang, Hui Liu
claim: The authors hypothesize and test that a good commit message contains both a Why (motivation) and a What (change summary). Across almost 1,600 messages from five active open source projects, about 44% could be improved; 'No Why' messages averaged 28%, about twice the 12% 'No What'. Why expressions fall into Describe Issue, Illustrate Requirement, Describe Objective and Imply Necessity. Messages whose Why is common sense, e.g. 'fix typo a->an', were not counted as missing Why.

title: SEURAT: Software Engineering Using RATionale (Eclipse plug-in; RationaleSchema.xml)
claim: SEURAT's RationaleSchema.xml defines requirement, decisionproblem, alternative, argument, claim, assumption, question, tradeoff and coOccurrence types (plus ontologies, constraints, contingencies, designer profiles and pattern library). Only four carry a status enum: requirement (Satisfied, Violated, Addressed, Retracted, Rejected, Undecided), decision problem (Resolved, Unresolved, Non-resolvable, Addressed, Retracted), alternative (Adopted, At_Issue, Rejected) and question (Unanswered, Answered). Those four each have a history of records with status, datestamp and reason. Decision problems have an optional string 'artifact' attribute tying them to a design element.

title: Web Annotation Data Model (W3C Recommendation)
authors: Robert Sanderson, Paolo Ciccarese, Benjamin Young (W3C)
claim: W3C Recommendation, 23 Feb 2017, editors Sanderson, Ciccarese, Young. TextQuoteSelector: exact required, prefix/suffix SHOULD be given, text MUST be normalized (tags SHOULD be removed). TextPositionSelector: start inclusive, end exclusive, described as very brittle to resource changes, and it is RECOMMENDED to add a State (e.g. TimeState) to identify the right representation. RangeSelector: startSelector and endSelector required and SHOULD be the same class; range runs from start up to but not including end. refinedBy chains selectors, each refining the previous result. Multiple selectors can describe the same segment to maximize later discoverability. A quote matching several places SHOULD be treated as matching all of them.

title: match-quote.ts (Hypothesis client anchoring)
claim: search() first loops text.indexOf for exact matches (errors: 0) and falls back to approxSearch only when none exist. maxErrors = Math.min(256, quote.length / 2). Weights: quote 50, prefix 20, suffix 20, position 2; score normalized by their sum (92); posScore = 1 - offset/text.length when a hint is given. Matches are sorted and the top one returned; null only for an empty quote or no candidates, despite a doc comment mentioning a minimum quality threshold. Comment cites expected cost O((maxErrors / 32) * text.length) from approx-string-match.

title: Robust Hyperlinks and Locations (D-Lib Magazine, July 2000)
claim: D-Lib Magazine vol. 6 no. 7/8, July/August 2000. Robust location stores a unique ID (author-supplied, element locations only), a tree walk (child numbers and tags from root, then word/char offsets in the leaf), and a context record with content before and after the location, up to 25 characters, possibly truncated at text element boundaries. Reattachment tries ID, then tree walk (alternating outward sibling search for matching node names, then assuming an added or removed level; each deviation adds weighted unreliability, failing past a client-set limit), then context search forward and backward, dropping context until a match or below a minimum length. Failure modes: IDs only where authors add them, sibling inserts or removals break walks, repeated word patterns confuse context. Unattached spans go to a floating note for manual repositioning ('Morph to Current Selection').

title: Robust Annotation Positioning in Digital Documents (MSR-TR-2000-95; CHI 2001)
authors: A.J. Bernheim Brush, David Bargeron, Anoop Gupta, JJ Cadiz
claim: MSR-TR-2000-95 (22 Sept 2000), also CHI 2001 pp. 285-292, DOI 10.1145/365024.365117. Table 1 classifies anchor edits as minor/medium/total delete, minor/medium/total reword, anchor-text move (indirect/direct) and paragraph move (indirect/direct). Second study: 12 participants, 216 annotations, 302 position ratings on a 7-point scale. Same and moved-but-unchanged anchors (121 ratings) got a median 7.0. For found changed anchors, modification score correlated with rating at -0.34 (p < .003). For orphaned anchors it correlated at .72 (p < .001), with total deletes at median 7.0. Participants stressed key words, proper names and quotations, and paid little attention to surrounding context. Authors suggest a 'best guess' feature that shows where orphaned annotations might belong.

title: Quantifying Orphaned Annotations in Hypothes.is
authors: Mohamed Aturban, Michael L. Nelson, Michele C. Weigle
claim: Of 20,953 Hypothes.is highlighted-text annotations, about 22% can no longer attach to the live page, and public web archives can reattach only about 12% of those. 53% of still-attached annotations would orphan if the live page changed. Authors conclude the target should be archived when the annotation is created.

title: Peritext: A CRDT for Rich-Text Collaboration
authors: Geoffrey Litt, Sarah Lim, Martin Kleppmann, Peter van Hardenberg (Ink & Switch)
claim: Format spans use opIds plus a before/after anchor type, not indexes, for start and end, so edits elsewhere do not move them. Bold grows when typing at its end; link and comment spans do not grow. Comments may overlap (several per character), unlike bold or color, which use last-write-wins. Deleted characters stay as tombstones and keep attached operations. Block elements (split, join, move) and moving/duplicating text such as cut/paste are left as future work.

title: Moving Elements in List CRDTs (PaPoC 2020)
claim: PaPoC '20, DOI 10.1145/3380787.3393677. Delete-and-reinsert duplicates an element under concurrent moves. A single-element move uses one LWW register per element holding its position ID. Moving a character range element by element leaves concurrent edits inside the range at the old position. Modeling each bullet point as its own text object makes split and join into moves of character ranges between objects. The paper says no known algorithm moves ranges of elements.

title: ProseMirror Reference: prosemirror-transform Position Mapping
claim: StepMap ranges are groups of three: [start, oldSize, newSize]. A Mapping is a pipeline of step maps, with invert(), appendMappingInverted(), and mirror support (mirror constructor arg, appendMap mirrors, getMirror) used when rebasing. map(pos, assoc) takes assoc -1 or 1 (default 1) to pick the side a position sticks to on insertion. mapResult returns a MapResult with pos, deleted, deletedBefore, deletedAfter and deletedAcross.

title: Y.RelativePosition (Yjs docs)
claim: A relative position is fixed to an element of the shared document, not an index. assoc >= 0 (default) binds to the character after the index, assoc < 0 to the character before. createAbsolutePositionFromRelativePosition returns {type, index, assoc}, or null when the position cannot be referenced or its type is deleted. After all clients sync, it resolves to the same index everywhere. Serializes via JSON.stringify/parse or encode/decodeRelativePosition (Uint8Array).

title: TEI P5 Guidelines, ch. 17 Linking, Segmentation, and Alignment: 17.9 Stand-off Markup
claim: Section 17.9 (ch. 17 Linking, Segmentation, and Alignment): in stand-off markup the text is included by reference (XInclude with XPointer; examples use string-range()). Uses: read-only source, several hierarchically incompatible markup schemes, multiple hierarchical ambiguities. Each overlapping hierarchy gets its own set of XInclude pointers to a common source. Without xi:fallback a missing resource is a fatal error, which is the preferred behavior; xi:fallback is not recommended for stand-off.

title: Pandoc User's Guide: Heading attributes, Divs and Spans
claim: header_attributes: headings take {#identifier .class key=value}; auto_identifiers derives IDs from heading text (with -1, -2 suffixes for duplicates). bracketed_spans: [text]{.class key="val"} becomes a Span with attributes. fenced_divs: a fence of at least three colons plus attributes opens a Div. Under link_attributes, unknown attributes pass through to HTML with data- prepended. The manual says writers generally don't use all of this information, and non-HTML/EPUB writers ignore unsupported attributes.

title: Obsidian Help: Internal links, Link to a block in a note
claim: A block ID is a space, caret and identifier at the end of a paragraph. For lists, quotes, callouts and tables it goes on its own line with blank lines around it, and a specific list item can carry one directly. Parts of quotes, callouts and tables cannot be linked. Typing ^ after a link suggests blocks, or you can write a readable ID like ^quote-of-the-day. Block references are not standard Markdown and do not work outside Obsidian.

title: git-blame documentation (-M, -C, --ignore-rev)
claim: -M detects lines moved or copied within a file (default num 20). -C detects lines from other files changed in the same commit (default 40); given twice it also searches the commit that created the file, three times any commit. num is the minimum alphanumeric characters to match. --ignore-rev blames changed lines on the previous commit that changed them or nearby lines. blame.markUnblamableLines marks lines it cannot reattribute with '*', and blame.markIgnoredLines marks reattributed lines with '?'.

title: SQLite FTS5 Extension
authors: SQLite project (D. Richard Hipp et al.)
claim: The trigram tokenizer enables substring matching and indexed LIKE/GLOB (not with remove_diacritics; only GLOB with case_sensitive 1; under 3 characters fails). The porter tokenizer stems English tokens. NEAR groups match phrases within N tokens (default 10). External content tables (content=) read column values from another table; the user keeps the index in sync, usually with triggers, and 'rebuild' regenerates it. bm25() ranks matches (lower is better), and highlight() and snippet() mark them. detail=column or none drops phrase and NEAR queries for a smaller index (743/340/134 MiB in the docs' test).

title: Hooks reference
claim: PreToolUse receives tool_name and tool_input (Edit: file_path, old_string, new_string, replace_all; Write: file_path, content). It can deny via permissionDecision or exit 2, add additionalContext, or rewrite arguments via updatedInput. PostToolUse receives tool_response and can add additionalContext, return decision block, or replace the result via updatedToolOutput, but the tool has already run. Stop with decision block keeps Claude working, subject to a cap of 8 consecutive continuations: the count resets each time Claude calls a tool, and CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP changes it. FileChanged fires on any on-disk change to a watched file, including changes from processes outside Claude Code, because it uses a filesystem watcher. It has no decision control and reads only watchPaths and systemMessage. additionalContext is capped at 10,000 characters. Matchers such as Edit|Write plus an `if` rule such as Edit(*.ts) scope a hook.

title: Plugin manifest reference
claim: A plugin is laid out as .claude-plugin/plugin.json plus root-level skills/, commands/, agents/, hooks/hooks.json and .mcp.json. CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT changes on every update. CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA (~/.claude/plugins/data/<id>/) persists across updates, and by default is deleted when the plugin is uninstalled from the last place it is installed. CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR is exported to hook processes. claude.ai and Cowork do not install a plugin that has a top-level bin/ directory. The automatic start of plugin MCP servers on enable is documented on the MCP page (https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp), not on this page.

title: MCP Specification 2026-07-28: Resources
claim: Resources are URI-identified and application-driven: the host decides how to include them. They support URI templates (resources/templates/list), notifications/resources/list_changed, per-resource notifications/resources/updated delivered through subscriptions/listen with resourceSubscriptions, and audience, priority and lastModified annotations. In the 2026-07-28 spec, requests are stateless and self-contained: every request carries protocolVersion and clientCapabilities in _meta.

title: Codex hooks
claim: Codex supports SessionStart, SessionEnd, SubagentStart, PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PostToolUse, PreCompact, PostCompact, UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStop, Stop and Interrupt hooks, with regex matchers. apply_patch can be matched as apply_patch, Edit or Write. PreToolUse can deny, add context or rewrite input (updatedInput). PostToolUse can add context, or with decision block replace the tool result with feedback. Stop can block, which makes Codex continue with an automatic continuation prompt.

title: Cursor agent hooks
claim: Cursor's agent hook events include preToolUse, postToolUse, afterFileEdit, beforeReadFile, sessionStart and stop, among others (beforeShellExecution, beforeMCPExecution, beforeSubmitPrompt, preCompact, subagentStart/Stop and more). afterFileEdit receives file_path and an edits array of old_string/new_string pairs. preToolUse and the before* hooks can deny, and exit code 2 blocks the action. postToolUse and sessionStart can add additional_context. stop can return a followup_message that Cursor submits automatically as the next user message, capped at 5 by default (loop_limit).

title: Co-Writing Screenplays and Theatre Scripts with Language Models: An Evaluation by Industry Professionals
authors: Piotr Mirowski, Kory W. Mathewson, Jaylen Pittman, Richard Evans
claim: Dramatron generates top-down through prompt chaining: log line, then title and characters, then plot beats and location descriptions, then dialogue per scene. Users can edit or regenerate at any level and go back to rewrite the log line. In a study with 15 theatre and film professionals, several participants said the top-down order fits screenwriting better than playwriting. Two self-identified playwrights (p4, p5) argued against the fixed hierarchy and said characters come last. Another participant (p9) said playwrights often find out what a play is about only after finishing it, and the authors suggest the log line could be a post-hoc summary.

title: DOC: Improving Long Story Coherence With Detailed Outline Control
authors: Kevin Yang, Dan Klein, Nanyun Peng, Yuandong Tian
claim: DOC adds a detailed outliner that builds a finer, hierarchically structured outline, plus a detailed controller that keeps generated passages faithful to the outline details. In human evaluations against Re3 it gained 22.5, 28.2 and 20.7 absolute points in plot coherence, outline relevance and interestingness. Raters judged it clearly more controllable in interactive generation.

title: PEER: A Collaborative Language Model
authors: Timo Schick, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Zhengbao Jiang, Fabio Petroni, Patrick Lewis, Gautier Izacard, Qingfei You, Christoforos Nalmpantis, Edouard Grave, Sebastian Riedel
claim: PEER (Plan, Edit, Explain, Repeat) models writing as repeated cycles of plan, edit and explain. A plan is a short instruction such as 'fix grammar errors', formed before the edit, and an explanation is written after it. The model is trained mainly on Wikipedia edit histories. Separate PEER-Undo (reverses edits to make synthetic history), PEER-Explain (writes explanations or plans) and PEER-Document (generates supporting documents) models infill missing parts, so the approach can self-train in domains without edit histories.

title: VISAR: A Human-AI Argumentative Writing Assistant with Visual Programming and Rapid Draft Prototyping
authors: Zheng Zhang, Jie Gao, Ranjodh Singh Dhaliwal, Toby Jia-Jun Li
claim: VISAR (UIST 2023) links a tree canvas of typed argument nodes to the editor. Node types: main argument, key aspect, discussion point, counterargument, supporting evidence. Edge types: featured by, elaborated by, attacked by, supported by. Canvas edits regenerate the draft, immediately or on Generate in Lazy mode, and VISAR prompts users to update dependent nodes recursively. Text reaches the canvas when the user selects it and clicks Add to graph, or adds a node directly. Paragraph order sometimes failed to update after nodes were reordered. Participants reported that draft prototypes led them back to the planning stage. Experts rated VISAR lower on Logic & Organization than the baseline (5.2 vs 6.9, p=.02).

title: Understanding Iterative Revision from Human-Written Text
authors: Wanyu Du, Vipul Raheja, Dhruv Kumar, Zae Myung Kim, Melissa Lopez, Dongyeop Kang
claim: IteraTeR annotates sentence- and paragraph-level edits across ArXiv, Wikipedia and Wikinews. The human-annotated set has 4,018 edits, labeled with these intents: fluency (23.44%), coherence (9.78%), clarity (39.85%) and style (3.19%), grouped as non-meaning-changed; meaning-changed (22.30%); and other (1.44%). It frames revision as iterative with a revision depth. Most edits occur at depth 1, the number drops rapidly at depth 2, and few edits occur at depths 3 and 4.

title: Structural Alignment as the Basis to Improve Significant Change Detection in Versioned Sentences (describes Faigley and Witte 1981, 'Analyzing Revision', CCC 32(4):400-414)
authors: Tan Ping Ping, Karin Verspoor, Timothy Miller (describing Lester Faigley and Stephen Witte)
claim: Tan, Verspoor and Miller (ALTA Workshop 2015, pp. 101-109) summarize Faigley and Witte's 1981 taxonomy (CCC 32(4):400-414). Surface changes improve readability without changing meaning and are split into formal changes (spelling, tense, format) and meaning-preserving changes (rephrasing). Text-base changes alter meaning: microstructure changes leave the text's summary intact, and macrostructure changes alter it. Tan et al. note that Faigley and Witte rely on an undefined notion of 'gist'. They describe another test for macro vs micro: whether the concepts in a change affect how other parts of the text read.

title: Beyond the Chat: Executable and Verifiable Text-Editing with LLMs
authors: Philippe Laban, Jesse Vig, Marti A. Hearst, Caiming Xiong, Chien-Sheng Wu
claim: InkSync stores each edit as JSON with original_text (must appear exactly in the draft, or the edit is discarded), replace_text, component, an optional replace_all and an optional new_info. Edits that add new information get a warning: the new_info flag agreed with manual labels on 97.5% of 200 sampled edits. A Verify step prompts an LLM to generate search queries. An audit view highlights system-generated text, traced with a character-level alignment algorithm. A suggestion is marked implicitly dismissed once its original_text no longer appears in the document.

title: Semantic Commit: Helping Users Update Intent Specifications for AI Memory at Scale
authors: Priyan Vaithilingam, Munyeong Kim, Frida-Cecilia Acosta-Parenteau, Daniel Lee, Amine Mhedhbi, Elena L. Glassman, Ian Arawjo
claim: SemanticCommit treats an intent specification (CLAUDE.md, Cursor rules, a game design document) as a list of discrete items. When new intent arrives, knowledge-graph retrieval (PageRank, HippoRAG-style) finds candidate items, and an LLM classifier labels them as direct conflict, ambiguous or no conflict. The system then proposes revising, deleting or flagging items, favoring recall over precision, and the user accepts or rejects each change. In a 12-person study, half the participants first flagged conflicts without AI revisions and then resolved them locally. Five participants skipped the parts the system did not flag.

title: Beyond Text Generation: Supporting Writers with Continuous Automatic Text Summaries
authors: Hai Dang, Karim Benharrak, Florian Lehmann, Daniel Buschek
claim: The editor shows a summary of each paragraph in the margin, continuously updated as the writer types, at levels ranging from full text to central sentences to keywords. In two studies (N=4, N=8) of analytic essays, the summaries gave writers an outside view of their text and helped them revise each paragraph's content and scope.

title: Codex Tracking
claim: Each Codex entry has a name and aliases. When tracking is on, every mention is underlined in the manuscript, plan and snippets, and counted in a mentions tracker. Each entry has an AI context policy: always include, include when detected (the default), don't include when detected, or never include. Matching is case-insensitive by default with an optional case-sensitive mode, and supports an exclusion list and auto-pluralisation for English-variant novels.

title: Specification-Driven Development (spec-driven.md, Spec Kit)
claim: Spec-driven development makes the specification the primary artifact and code its expression: changes start in the spec, and implementation plans and code are continuously regenerated from it. Updated acceptance criteria make implementation plans flag affected technical decisions. AI checks specs for ambiguity, contradictions and gaps, and consistency validation runs continuously. The document says practicing SDD today requires assembling existing tools and keeping discipline.

title: Telling More Than We Can Know: Verbal Reports on Mental Processes
authors: Richard E. Nisbett, Timothy DeCamp Wilson
claim: The review finds evidence that there may be little or no direct introspective access to higher-order cognitive processes. When people report why they responded as they did, they do not use true introspection. Their reports rest on a priori, implicit causal theories or on judgments of how plausible a stimulus is as a cause. So reports are accurate when the influential stimuli are salient and plausible causes, and inaccurate when they are not.

title: Verbal Reports as Data
authors: K. Anders Ericsson, Herbert A. Simon
claim: When subjects think aloud, they verbalize information they are attending to in short-term memory, and such reports are data. Verbalizing affects cognitive processes only when instructions require reporting information that would not otherwise be attended to. Inaccurate reports in other research come from asking for information that was never directly heeded, which forces subjects to infer rather than remember their mental processes.

title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
authors: Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, Samuel R. Bowman
claim: Biasing features in the input, such as reordering options so the answer is always (A), heavily steer chain-of-thought answers. Models do not mention these features and instead rationalize the biased answer. Accuracy dropped by as much as 36% across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0. The explanations can be plausible yet misleading.

title: Freewriting (excerpt from Writing Without Teachers, Oxford UP, pp. 1-7)
claim: Almost everyone edits while producing words. This compulsive, premature editing makes writing blocked, hard, and dead, because it damps out voice. Freewriting is nonediting: it undoes the habit of editing while producing. Editing is still necessary, but it belongs afterward. Trying to get the beginning just right is a formula for failure.

title: Knowing-in-Action: The New Scholarship Requires a New Epistemology
claim: Schön draws on Polanyi's tacit knowing and argues that everyday and professional competence is mostly tacit knowing-in-action. When people try to describe it they find themselves at a loss, or they misstate it. Asking them mainly reveals what they know about answering such a question, so you must observe them in action. Surprise triggers reflection-in-action. Reflecting afterward on reflection-in-action, as a player does reviewing game video, makes the implicit strategies and assumptions explicit.

title: Hypermedia Support for Argumentation-Based Rationale: 15 Years on from gIBIS and QOC
authors: Simon J. Buckingham Shum, Albert M. Selvin, Maarten Sierhuis, Jeffrey Conklin, Charles B. Haley, Bashar Nuseibeh
claim: The capture problem is the spectre haunting all design-rationale efforts: how to get quality rationale in without disrupting the work it serves. Citing Grudin, the authors say there cannot be a disparity between who invests effort and who benefits, so there must be immediate value. Reports of 'cognitive overhead' emerged soon after NoteCards and gIBIS. A study of designers learning QOC traced it to four interleaved tasks: unbundling, classification, naming, and structuring. Rationale does not come 'for free'.

title: Formality Considered Harmful: Experiences, Emerging Themes, and Directions on the Use of Formal Representations in Interactive Systems
authors: Frank M. Shipman III, Catherine C. Marshall
claim: Across experiences with hypertext, knowledge-based, and collaborative systems, users resisted formal structure for four reasons: cognitive overhead, tacit knowledge, premature structure, and situated structure. The authors say users are often justified in rejecting formalisms. They recommend formalizing only what is essential for the task, weighing extra structure as an optional cost/benefit trade-off, supporting gradual or incremental formalization, and inferring implicit structure from textual, spatial, or temporal patterns.

title: On the Relationship between Comment Update Practices and Software Bugs
authors: Walid M. Ibrahim, Nicolas Bettenburg, Bram Adams, Ahmed E. Hassan
claim: In FreeBSD, PostgreSQL, and Eclipse, comment update practices explained and predicted future bugs better than the number of prior bugs or changes. Inconsistent changes were not necessarily correlated with more bugs. The risky signal was a function and its comment suddenly being updated inconsistently when they are usually updated together, or the reverse. The authors quote Siy et al.: once developers find one inconsistent comment, they lose confidence in the rest and ignore them.

title: Building a Discourse-Tagged Corpus in the Framework of Rhetorical Structure Theory
authors: Lynn Carlson, Daniel Marcu, Mary Ellen Okurowski
claim: Building the RST Corpus took more than a dozen full- or part-time people over one year (2000). The annotators were professional language analysts given extensive training, and the final tagging manual ran to over 80 pages. Annotating one document took 30 minutes to several hours. In the final pairwise results, kappa was about 0.95-1.0 for units (segmentation) but about 0.60-0.79 for relations. The authors attribute the extra difficulty to RST's rich relation set and interpretive nuclearity. Decisions are easy between clauses, more complex between sentences, and extremely difficult when linking large segments.

title: A Problem for RST: The Need for Multi-Level Discourse Analysis
authors: Johanna D. Moore, Martha E. Pollack
claim: RST presumes a single preferred rhetorical relation between consecutive discourse elements, but elements are related simultaneously on multiple levels, both informational and intentional. The single-relation assumption is one reason RST analyses are inherently ambiguous. It also loses the intentional structure needed to elaborate or clarify an utterance, for example in answering follow-up questions. A multi-label fix fails because intentional and informational relations have no one-to-one mapping.

title: Attentional Overload and Writing Performance: Effects of Rough Draft and Outline Strategies
claim: Preparing a written outline led to higher-quality documents than no outline. Writing a rough draft instead of a polished draft did not improve quality. A mental outline helped as much as a written one. Both kinds of outline eased attentional overload and let writers spend more processing time translating ideas into text, though not more cognitive effort.

title: Review of Toward a Composition Made Whole by Jody Shipka (on her multimodal goal statement)
authors: Brandy Dieterle (review of Jody Shipka, University of Pittsburgh Press, 2011)
claim: In her book, Shipka has students submit a statement of goals and choices. The review quotes her saying students detail how, why, and under what conditions they made their rhetorical, technological, and methodological choices (p. 113). According to the review, these statements raise awareness of writing strategies that are sometimes invisible. They also give Shipka a way to navigate and respond to texts that do not look or work like the forms she knows.

title: Can AI writing be salvaged? Mitigating Idiosyncrasies and Improving Human-AI Alignment in the Writing Process through Edits (CHI 2025; arXiv 2409.14509)
authors: Tuhin Chakrabarty, Philippe Laban, Chien-Sheng Wu
claim: 18 professional writers edited 1,057 LLM-generated creative paragraphs (the LAMP corpus), producing 8,035 span edits. A formative study gave a seven-category taxonomy: cliché, unnecessary/redundant exposition, purple prose, poor sentence structure, lack of specificity and detail, awkward word choice and phrasing, tense inconsistency. The most common were awkward word choice (28%), poor sentence structure (20%), unnecessary exposition (18%) and clichés (17%). The distribution was similar for GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Llama 3.1 70B. Edits were 74% replacements, 18% deletions and 8% insertions. 70% of non-deletion edits were meaning-preserving by BERTScore, and the authors say the split is a continuum.

title: A Truth Maintenance System (MIT AI Memo AIM-521; Artificial Intelligence 12(3), 1979)
claim: Per the memo abstract, reasoning programs must make assumptions and revise beliefs when discoveries contradict them. The TMS is a subsystem that records and maintains the reasons for program beliefs, and uses them to explain the program's actions and guide the problem solver. Its belief-revision mechanisms update the current belief set, and dependency-directed backtracking changes the current set of assumptions. The companion memo AIM-461 (1978, https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/6287) describes these reasons as fragments of deductions, used as partial proofs to keep the belief database consistent.

title: Scorekeeping in a Language Game (Journal of Philosophical Logic 8:339-359)
claim: At each stage a conversation has a score, whose components are abstract entities such as sets of presupposed propositions and boundaries of permissible action. Whether a move is correct, and even a sentence's acceptability, depends on the current score. The score evolves by rules of kinematics: the score at a later stage is fixed by the earlier score and what was said in between. Unlike baseball, conversational score tends to shift so that whatever occurs counts as correct play. Under the rule of accommodation for presupposition, if something said needs P and P is absent, P comes into existence, ceteris paribus, within limits, and provided nobody objects. Order matters: 'All Fred's children are asleep, and Fred has children' is odd because the first clause already created the presupposition.

title: Toward a Model of Text Comprehension and Production (Psychological Review 85(5):363-394)
authors: Walter Kintsch, Teun A. van Dijk
claim: Discourse semantics has two levels. The microstructure is individual propositions and their relations, and the macrostructure is the global topic or gist. Macrorules connect them. Deletion: a proposition may be deleted if it is not a direct or indirect interpretation condition of a later proposition. Generalization: a sequence may be replaced by a proposition denoting its immediate superset. Construction: a sequence may be replaced by a global fact of which the facts are normal conditions, components or consequences. The rules apply recursively, giving several macro levels, and the macrostructure must be entailed by the microstructure. A schema that formalizes the reader's goals controls which information counts as relevant. Coherence requires both local connection and global organization. Producing recall and summaries partly inverts the macro-operators.

title: The Intentional Fallacy (Sewanee Review 54(3):468-488), Michigan Tech electronic reserve reproduction
authors: W. K. Wimsatt Jr., Monroe C. Beardsley
claim: The author's design or intention is neither available nor desirable as a standard for judging a literary work. If the author succeeded, the work itself shows what he intended. If he failed, the work is not adequate evidence of the intention. The poem is public language, detached from its author, and is judged like a pudding or a machine, by whether it works. The authors separate internal evidence (the text, its semantics and syntax, public language) from external evidence (journals, letters, reported conversations about composition). Authors' accounts of how they wrote belong to psychology or craft advice, not criticism. Practical messages differ: they succeed when the reader correctly infers the intention.

title: PROV-DM: The PROV Data Model (W3C Recommendation, 30 April 2013)
authors: Luc Moreau, Paolo Missier (eds.), W3C Provenance Working Group
claim: The core types are Entity (a thing with fixed aspects), Activity (something over time that acts on entities) and Agent (bears responsibility). The relations are: wasGeneratedBy and used; wasDerivedFrom, with subtypes Revision, Quotation and PrimarySource; wasAttributedTo (entity to agent); wasAssociatedWith (agent responsible for an activity, optionally with a plan); actedOnBehalfOf (delegation, where the responsible agent keeps some responsibility); wasInvalidatedBy (start of an entity's destruction or expiry, after which it can no longer be used); and specializationOf and alternateOf.

title: Measuring and Controlling Instruction (In)Stability in Language Model Dialogs (COLM 2024; arXiv 2402.10962)
authors: Kenneth Li, Tianle Liu, Naomi Bashkansky, David Bau, Fernanda Viégas, Hanspeter Pfister, Martin Wattenberg
claim: A benchmark has two instructed chatbots talk to each other and then tests whether each still follows its system prompt. Models including LLaMA2-chat-70B and GPT-3.5 drifted significantly from their instructions within eight rounds. The authors attribute part of the drift to the transformer's attention to the initial instructions decaying as the dialog grows, and propose split-softmax as a lightweight mitigation.

title: Politics and the English Language (Horizon, April 1946), Orwell Foundation text
claim: For every sentence, a careful writer asks four questions: what is my meaning, which words express it, which image or idiom makes it clearer, and is that image fresh enough to have an effect. Two more probably follow: can it be said more briefly, and is anything needlessly ugly. Six rules follow: avoid figures of speech often seen in print; use the short word; cut any word that can be cut; prefer the active voice; prefer everyday English to foreign, scientific or jargon terms; break any of these rules rather than write something barbarous.

title: Vale documentation: Styles (checks, rule fields, vocabularies)
claim: A rule is a YAML file that extends one of 12 checks: existence, substitution, occurrence, repetition, consistency, conditional, capitalization, metric, readability, spelling, sequence and script. Consistency reports a file that uses two forms of the same thing. Substitution reports a pattern and carries its replacement. Conditional reports a pattern that appears without another pattern it depends on. Occurrence reports too few or too many matches. Every rule has a required message, an optional link to the guidance it enforces, and a level (suggestion, warning or error; only errors set a non-zero exit code). Scope defaults to text, and heading is one other value. Project vocabularies list accepted and rejected terms, enforced by Vale.Terms and Vale.Avoid.

title: 「指差呼称」のエラー防止効果の室内実験による検証 (Laboratory experiments for verifying the effectiveness of 'finger-pointing and call' as a practical tool of human error prevention), 産業・組織心理学研究 9(2):107-114
authors: Shigeru Haga, Hajime Akatsuka, Hiroaki Shiroto (Railway Technical Research Institute)
claim: PRIMARY SOURCE of the '1994 RTRI study'. JR West asked RTRI in 1994 for new data for an employee training video. The paper was partly presented in 1995. Exp I: 24 RTRI employees (4 women, age 21-31), within-subjects, counterbalanced. They faced a cab mock-up with a CRT 2.4 m away showing one of 5 coloured 'signals' every 2 s and pressed the matching one of 5 keys; 100 scored trials per condition. Mean errors per 100 trials: neither 2.375 (SD 3.536), pointing only 0.750, calling only 1.000, pointing and calling 0.375 (SD 0.924), an 84% drop. ANOVA p<.01. Dunnett vs neither: pointing only and pointing+calling p<.01, calling only not significant. Participants with at least one error: 15/24 vs 5/24 (chi-square p<.05). Cost: mean RT rose from 0.751 s to 1.074 s (p<.01). Exp II (habitual 'pulled-in' error): after 100 non-red signals, the first red came at trial 101; 5/12 pressed anyway without pointing and calling vs 0/12 with it (Fisher p<.05). History (citing Kanto Railway Academy 1970): signal calling began spontaneously early in Japanese rail as driver-fireman call and response; JNR first mandated it in its rules in 1947; crews near Tokyo added pointing from the early Showa era (late 1920s); pointing was codified regionally in 1970. JNR/JR name: 指差喚呼 (shisa kanko). JISHA added it to the Zero Accident campaign in 1981. The authors say the data cannot confirm or deny the textbook mechanisms. Their impression is that the inserted action and its time lag suppressed hasty and habitual responses. They warn against generalizing to other tasks, against forcing it so often that it turns into an empty ritual, and against using it to shift safety responsibility onto workers.

title: 指差呼称のエラー防止機能 (Error prevention function of finger pointing and call), 日本認知心理学会発表論文集 2009
authors: Masayoshi Shigemori, Tomoe Saito, Mizuki Tatebayashi, Aya Mizutani, Takayuki Masuda, Shigeru Haga (RTRI; Rikkyo University)
claim: Conference abstract with 50 students, testing three proposed functions. (1) Number comparison: pointing and calling cut errors as much as a plain enforced pause (a 1.5 s no-response sign) did, so the time lag before responding is confirmed as a mechanism. (2) n-back: calling helped at n=1 but hurt at n=3, like articulatory suppression, so the memory effect is mixed. (3) Number search: pointing did not reduce errors, so the attention-focusing function was not confirmed.

title: 指差呼称の効果に関する基礎研究(2): タスク・スイッチング (Fundamental study of the effect of finger-pointing and call (2): Task Switching), 日本心理学会第75回大会発表論文集 1EV131
authors: Kazumitsu Shinohara, Hiroshi Naito, Yuko Matsui, Masaru Hikono (Osaka University; INSS)
claim: Conference precursor of the 2013 IJIE paper. 20 participants (10 men, 10 women, mean age 25) judged digit pairs by one of three rules (value, size, position), each cued before the trial; the conditions were pointing and calling the rule cue vs not. On rule-switch trials, responses without pointing and calling were significantly slower (about 575 vs 510 ms; interaction F(1,38)=12.17, p<.001). Accuracy did not differ by pointing and calling. Rated workload did not increase. Conclusion: calling out the rule activates it, so the same accuracy comes faster with no extra burden.

title: The effects of 'finger pointing and calling' on cognitive control processes in the task-switching paradigm, International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics 43(2):129-136
authors: Kazumitsu Shinohara, Hiroshi Naito, Yuko Matsui, Masaru Hikono
claim: Peer-reviewed follow-up. Citation confirmed via Crossref; the abstract is paywalled and ScienceDirect returned 403. Secondary summaries (Semantic Scholar TLDR, search snippet) say 20 participants made binary decisions on two digits under one of three cued rules. They also say finger pointing and calling aids cognitive control in the supervisory attentional system, is most useful when a signal requires choosing among memorized alternatives, and is effective against operational errors when cognitive control is needed. These claims rest only on secondary summaries.
